dateline: FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 13, 2026 · Pre-Dawn: New Low, New Reason
headline: NEW LOW, NEW REASON.

bullets.html: Dec Chicago closed Thursday at $5.82½, down 18¼¢, the lowest close of the move and under last Friday's $5.85 low. Kansas City lost 20½¢ to $6.19. Minneapolis lost 13½¢ to $6.22. One session erased Tuesday's and Wednesday's 13¼¢ bounce and 5¢ more.
Overnight, most of it came back. Dec Chicago was $5.95¼, up 12¾¢, at 1:58 a.m. Pacific. Kansas City was $6.31¼, up 12¼¢. A close above $5.90½ today would end a ten-week losing streak.

The seller changed on Thursday. The dollar index traded above 103, its highest since April 2025, after Tuesday's hot October CPI. Fed funds futures put the odds of a December rate hike near 85%. Gold lost $121. Corn and soybeans fell too.

Abu Dhabi ended Wednesday with a prisoner exchange and nothing on shipping. Thursday the U.S. envoys spent about two hours with Putin in Moscow, then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy. No ship has moved.
Minneapolis closed above Kansas City. On Monday KC was 10½¢ over Minneapolis. Thursday it was 3¢ under. USDA now projects hard red winter exports as the second lowest on record.

Tuesday's WASDE: U.S. ending stocks 743 million bu, up 3 million. Exports unchanged at 750 million. White wheat exports raised, and white wheat stocks cut from 80 million bu to 70 million. World stocks 280.8 MMT, above every trade guess.
Portland soft white bid $6.25 for November, about 42½¢ over Dec Chicago (Northwest Grain Growers). Since Monday the board is down a nickel and the soft white bid is up a nickel.

Paris ran up to its own Box-o-Rox line Wednesday and turned back Thursday, to €231.75, down €4.25. From the Sept. 2 highs, Chicago is down 26.7%. Paris is down 7.2%. Algeria bought more than 700,000 tonnes this week (UkrAgroConsult).

Box-o-Rox: EXECUTE. Thursday was the 27th straight close below the Suspend/Execute line, now $6.79¼, 96¾¢ above Thursday's close. Box-o-Rox informs; the marketing plan decides. See the chart and the rules →
Ahead: weekly export sales at 5:30 a.m. Pacific today, a day late for Veterans Day (trade range 350,000 to 650,000 tonnes). The COT report moves to Monday.

body.html: For three weeks Chicago wheat sold a peace that hadn't happened. This week the peace table adjourned without one, and Chicago made a new low anyway. Dec closed Thursday at $5.82½, down 18¼¢. That's under last Friday's $5.85 low and under Monday's $5.87½ close, so it's the lowest close of the move. It also took back the whole bounce. Dec had gained 4¢ Tuesday and 9¼¢ Wednesday, to $6.00¾, its first close above $6.00 since Nov. 2. Thursday's session traded as high as $6.03 on Wednesday night and fell to $5.82¼ in the final half hour, with the heaviest selling into the close. It settled a quarter cent off the low. Dec is now $2.12½ under the Sept. 2 high of $7.95, down 26.7%.

Then the night session took most of it back. Dec Chicago climbed steadily from the open and was $5.95¼, up 12¾¢, at 1:58 a.m. Pacific. Kansas City was $6.31¼, up 12¼¢, at 1:29 a.m. No single headline explains it, and a market that drops 18¼¢ with this many shorts in it doesn't need one to bounce. Here's what the bounce puts in play: last Friday's close was $5.90½. If Dec holds above that through today's close, the ten-week losing streak ends. That's a big if, with export sales due at 5:30 a.m. Pacific.

Start with what this week's bounce was. The Abu Dhabi talks ran Tuesday and Wednesday and produced an agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange, per Al Jazeera and Meduza. Jared Kushner called it "a very tough meeting but a productive one" and said territory was "the hardest" issue. Vladimir Medinsky said "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia." Neither report mentions grain, ports or shipping lanes. Wheat's Wednesday gain came as the market worked that out, per The Grain Ledger: two days of talks, one prisoner swap, no deal on Black Sea shipping. For two sessions the peace trade ran in reverse, and Chicago led the U.S. wheats higher.

Then Thursday arrived with a different seller. The dollar index traded above 103, its highest since April 2025, per Trading Economics and CNBC. The fuel was Tuesday's October CPI: prices rose 0.4% on the month, and core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Fed funds futures now put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec. 9 near 85%, with most of the remainder on a half point. A stronger dollar raises the price of U.S. wheat for every buyer who pays in another currency, and Thursday it hit nearly everything priced in dollars. Gold lost $121.70. Dec corn fell 5½¢. January soybeans fell 11¾¢. Brownfield's headline called it profit taking. Crude oil went the other way, up $2.21 to $88.74, so this wasn't an energy story. It was a currency story.

That matters for how to read the new low. Until Wednesday, the argument against the selling was simple: Chicago was pricing a handshake that hadn't happened. The handshake still hasn't happened, and Thursday's close was lower anyway. The market found a second reason. A reason that comes out of Abu Dhabi can reverse on one headline. A reason that comes out of the Federal Reserve takes longer to reverse, because the Fed doesn't meet until Dec. 8–9 and nothing on the calendar between now and then is scheduled to argue with a 0.3% core print.

On Tuesday we pointed at the crowd: open interest in Chicago wheat near a one-year high, with funds short. We said every one of those contracts has to be bought back someday. Wednesday looked like some of that buying. Thursday took it back, and the overnight looks like buying again. Three reversals in three sessions is what a crowded market does when it loses its reason and goes looking for another. The next hard evidence on who is doing what is the CFTC's Commitments of Traders report, pushed to Monday by the holiday.

Tuesday's WASDE was the quiet one, as advertised, with two numbers worth keeping. USDA put U.S. wheat ending stocks at 743 million bushels, up 3 million from October and under the 747 million the trade expected, per DTN. Exports stayed at 750 million. On Tuesday we wrote that with inspections running 36% behind last year against a forecast that assumes a 17% decline, either the ships speed up or the forecast comes down. USDA chose neither. It did move the classes inside that total. White wheat exports went up on what USDA called continued strong sales and shipments to Asia. Hard red winter exports went down and are now projected as the second lowest on record. White wheat ending stocks dropped from 80 million bushels to 70 million. Hard red winter stocks rose from 333 million to 344 million, per Ag Optimus's table of the report. USDA also trimmed the season-average farm price a dime, to $6.20.

The world table carried the surprise. USDA raised global wheat ending stocks to 280.8 MMT from 276.0. The highest guess in the trade survey was 278.6, per DTN. World production rose 5.1 MMT on bigger crops in Argentina (23.0 MMT), Australia (32.5), Kazakhstan and Ukraine. Read the behavior behind the stocks number, though. USDA cut Russia's exports by 1 MMT to 39 MMT, against 48 MMT last year, and cut Ukraine's by 1 MMT to 11.5 MMT. It blamed continued disruption in the Black Sea. Russia's own ending stocks rose by the same million tonnes. Part of that big world carryout is wheat sitting behind a closed port. The wheat exists. Whether it can get to a buyer is the question Abu Dhabi didn't answer.

Now the oddball. Minneapolis closed above Kansas City on Thursday: $6.22 against $6.19. On Monday, KC was 10½¢ over Minneapolis. KC took the hardest hit of the three on Thursday, down 20½¢, two days after USDA wrote "second lowest on record" next to its export line. KC's premium over Chicago narrowed to 36½¢ from 44½¢ on Monday. On Tuesday we said Chicago had fallen out of phase with the other wheats and asked which side would do the catching up. This week's answer: Kansas City came down to meet Chicago. Chicago didn't rise to meet Kansas City. KC's low on Thursday was $6.18¾, less than 8¢ above the June 30 low at $6.11.

Paris finally blinked, a little. Euronext Dec milling wheat climbed four sessions in a row, ran up to its own Box-o-Rox line near €236.75 on Wednesday, and turned back Thursday to close at €231.75, down €4.25. It's still about €6 above last Friday's close. From the Sept. 2 highs, Chicago is down 26.7% and Paris is down 7.2%. A week ago that gap was 16 points. It's more than 19 now. And the buyers came to that side of the ocean: Algeria bought more than 700,000 tonnes of milling wheat this week, per UkrAgroConsult, and China booked French and Argentine cargoes, per The Grain Ledger. The world bought wheat at these prices. It didn't buy much of ours. Total Farm Marketing put it plainly on Wednesday: the U.S. hasn't picked up as many of the missed Black Sea exports as the trade hoped. A dollar at a 19-month high doesn't help. This morning's export sales report is the next read on it.

The diplomacy didn't stop on Wednesday. It moved. Steve Witkoff and Kushner met Putin at the Kremlin for about two hours Thursday, per the Associated Press, and Putin again called European peacekeepers in Ukraine "absolutely unacceptable." The envoys then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy, who said Europe will be part of the next round, per the Irish Times. Ukraine's David Arakhamia talked about "good momentum" toward a deal before year-end. Meanwhile a Ukrainian drone attack hit Russia's Baltic port of Ust-Luga, per Total Farm Marketing. That's the route Moscow has leaned on for grain since the southern ports slowed in August. The peace headline isn't gone. It can come back any morning, from Moscow, Dublin or Washington, and Chicago has shown how it trades one.

Our class did more than hold its bid this week. It raised it. Northwest Grain Growers bid November soft white at $6.25 for Portland on Thursday, about 42½¢ over Dec Chicago. On Monday the Portland bid was $6.20 and 32½¢ over. On Oct. 23 it was even with the board. Since Monday, Dec Chicago is down a nickel and the soft white bid is up a nickel. Tuesday's WASDE explains why: USDA raised white wheat exports and cut white wheat stocks by 10 million bushels. The Portland bid has been saying that for three weeks. Now it's in the government's table. One more number to set beside it: USDA's season-average farm price for all U.S. wheat is $6.20. Thursday's Portland soft white bid was above it.
Scout the terrain, redrawn. These levels are for Dec Chicago.

Overhead: $5.95 to $5.97½ comes first. That's where the overnight bounce stood at 2 a.m. Pacific and where Thursday's day session failed. Next, $6.00¾ to $6.03¾: Wednesday's close and this week's highs. Beyond that, $6.10, the 20-day average, marked "Tripwire" on the Box-o-Rox chart.
Underfoot: $5.85, last Friday's low. Then Thursday's low at $5.82¼, the June 15 summer low at $5.70 on our continuation chart, and the April 10 low at $5.67½.

On our daily chart, the 55-session downtrend line from the Aug. 28 high close runs in the low $5.80s this morning. Thursday closed right on it. The overnight trade is about a dime above it. A trade isn't a close. A close back above $5.87½ says Thursday was a dollar day and not a new leg down. A close under Thursday's low says the market is headed for the summer lows. In Kansas City, the June 30 low at $6.11 is 8¢ below Thursday's close. In Minneapolis, the Feb. 27 line at $5.98½ is 23½¢ below. It's a map, not a forecast.

Box-o-Rox: EXECUTE. Thursday was the 27th straight close below the Suspend/Execute line, which now sits at $6.79¼, 96¾¢ above Thursday's close. No discretionary hold is in effect. The line is falling better than a cent a day, so the gap narrows from above even when price does nothing. The benchmark's record is on the chart: 83% of the 2026 crop was priced as of Oct. 1.
Marketing posture: EXECUTE, on plan. Today's question: the market's reason changed this week. Did anything in your plan?

• Producers: Chicago made a new low close Thursday and the Portland soft white bid went up. If you grow soft white, $6.25 is a nickel better than Monday's bid and above USDA's $6.20 season average. Check your resting offers against the cash bid this morning, not against the Chicago headline. If you grow hard red winter, the news runs the other way: KC lost 20½¢ Thursday and USDA just cut your export line. Call the elevator and ask whether basis moved with the board. The overnight bounce gives every offer resting just above the market a second look today. EXECUTE says offers at your plan's numbers are live.

• Unpriced wheat in the bin: On Monday we said to run the carry with a quarter point added to the operating line. The December hike was a what-if then. At 85% odds it's the base case. If the bin doesn't clear the interest at the higher rate, it's costing you money to hold it.

• Millers, feeders and end users: This week showed both sides of a crowded market: 13¼¢ up in two sessions, 18¼¢ down in one, 12¾¢ back overnight. Thursday's close was the cheapest of the move, $2.12½ off the high. If coverage is thin, scale it in. Don't wait for one perfect day. Hard red winter buyers have the better opening: KC's premium over Chicago narrowed 8¢ this week.

• Merchandisers: Watch five things today and into the weekend:
  – Export sales at 5:30 a.m. Pacific. The trade range is 350,000 to 650,000 tonnes. With Chicago more than 19 points cheaper than Paris since Labor Day, a number at the low end is a problem.
  – The Minneapolis–KC spread. Minneapolis was 3¢ over on Thursday. Does it hold?
  – Dec Chicago's close against $5.87½ and against last Friday's $5.90½.
  – The dollar index against Thursday's high above 103.
  – Weekend headlines out of Moscow and Dublin. There's no meeting on the calendar, which means there's no warning either.

• Lenders and elevator managers: Mark unpriced Chicago-priced inventory at $5.82½, then run it at $5.80 and $5.70. Mark soft white at the Portland bid. Thursday they were 42½¢ apart. Use a quarter point higher on operating lines for December as the working assumption, and run a half point as the stress case. Fertilizer hasn't given anything back: at $1,007 a ton, per DTN's late-October survey, anhydrous still costs about 161 bushels of soft white at $6.25, before freight.

Here's the part of Thursday that reaches the kitchen table. The same inflation report that pushed the dollar up and wheat down is the one that will help set the rate on next spring's operating note. The price of the crop and the cost of carrying it moved against the grower in the same session, for the same reason. Nobody in Abu Dhabi, Moscow or Dublin caused that, and nobody there can fix it. What you can do is what you did before any of it: know your number, know your bid, and know what the note costs at a quarter point higher. A plan written for a market that was selling peace still works in a market that's selling the dollar, because the plan was never about the reason. It was about the price. Somebody wrote the first marketing plan on your place long before there was a dollar index to watch. The tools have changed since then. The job hasn't: get this crop sold at a price that puts the next one in the ground.

This stuff is trackable. Let's track it.
Stay tuned.
—Gabe
